chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Door with No Bell
chapters.text:
Mr Utterson the lawyer was a serious, quiet man who almost never smiled and never used three words when one was enough. And yet people liked him. He was always slow to judge others, and when his friends got into trouble, he was often the last respectable man who still opened his door to them. “I let my brother go to the devil in his own way,” he liked to say.

Every Sunday he went for a long walk through London with his cousin, Mr Richard Enfield. They hardly spoke on these walks and often looked bored. However, neither of them would miss a Sunday for anything.

One Sunday their walk took them down a small street in a busy part of the city. The shops were bright and clean, but near one corner stood a strange, ugly building. It had no windows at all — only a door, with no bell and no knocker. The paint was old, and nobody ever seemed to clean it.

Enfield lifted his walking stick and pointed. “Have you ever noticed that door?” he asked. “In my mind it's connected with a very odd story.”

“Really?” said Utterson. “What story?”

“I was coming home at about three o'clock on a black winter morning,” Enfield began. “The streets were completely empty and as silent as a church. Then I saw two figures. One was a little man who was walking fast. The other was a girl of eight or ten, running down a side street. They ran into each other at the corner. And then came the horrible part. The man walked calmly over the child's body and left her screaming on the ground. He didn't stop. He didn't even look down. It wasn't like a man at all. It was like some terrible machine.”

Utterson said nothing, but he walked a little more slowly.

“I ran after him, caught him by the collar and brought him back. By then a crowd had gathered around the child — her family, and a doctor. Thank God, the girl wasn't badly hurt. But here's the strange thing. Everyone hated that man at first sight. Even the doctor, a quiet, ordinary sort of person, went white with the wish to kill him. So we told the man that we would make his name stink from one end of London to the other — unless he paid the family a hundred pounds.”

“And did he?”

“He did. He stood there among us with a black, cold smile, as if nothing could touch him. Then he led us to — where do you think? To that door. He took out a key, went inside and came back with ten pounds in gold and a cheque for the rest. The name on the cheque was a famous one — the name of a very good and respected man. I was sure the cheque was false, but the next morning the bank paid it without question.”

“And the man who walked over the child,” said Utterson slowly. “What was his name?”

“Hyde. Edward Hyde.”

Utterson's face did not move. “What does he look like?”

Enfield thought for a long time. “That's the odd thing,” he said at last. “I can't describe him. There's something wrong with him — something unpleasant, something hateful. He gives you the feeling that his body is twisted somehow, and yet it isn't. I've never seen a man I disliked so much, and I don't know why. I can see him now in my mind, as clearly as I see you. And still I can't tell you what he looks like.”

“You're sure he used a key?”

“Quite sure. And he still has it. I saw him go in again not a week ago.”

Utterson sighed. “Richard, let's make a promise. Let's never speak of this again.”

“With all my heart,” said Enfield, and they shook hands on it.

But Utterson could not stop thinking about the story. He had already guessed the name on the cheque. And the name Edward Hyde was not new to him either. It was written in a document that lay, at that very moment, in the safe in his own office.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Mr Hyde and Mr Seek
chapters.text:
That evening Utterson opened his safe and took out an envelope marked “Dr Jekyll's Will”. A will is the document that says who will get a person's money and property after his death. Utterson had always hated this one. It said that if Henry Jekyll died, everything he owned would go to “my friend Edward Hyde”. Stranger still, if Dr Jekyll disappeared for more than three months, for any reason at all, Edward Hyde would take his place at once.

“I used to think it was just madness,” Utterson said to himself. “Now I'm afraid it's something much worse.”

That night he hardly slept. He kept seeing the dark, empty streets, the little man, the child falling. Then he saw a bedroom where his friend Jekyll lay asleep. The door opened, a figure stood beside the bed, and Jekyll had to get up and obey it. In all these dreams the figure had no face.

“If I could see his face just once, the mystery would disappear,” Utterson thought. So he began to watch the door with no bell. He waited near it in the morning, at noon, and late at night under the moon. “If he is Mr Hyde,” he said with a dry little smile, “then I shall be Mr Seek.” Hide-and-seek is a children's game. But this was no game.

At last, on a cold, clear night, he heard footsteps — light, quick and somehow strange. A small man came round the corner and took a key from his pocket.

Utterson stepped forward and touched his shoulder. “Mr Hyde, I think?”

The man jumped back with a hiss, like a snake. “That's my name,” he said coldly, without looking up. “What do you want?”

“I'm an old friend of Dr Jekyll's. My name is Utterson. Will you let me see your face?”

Hyde waited a moment. Then he looked up. He was pale and small. He smiled, but the smile was ugly, and when he spoke, his voice was soft and broken, almost a whisper. Utterson felt cold with disgust.

“Now you'll know me again,” said Hyde. “That may be useful.” And he gave Utterson his address in Soho, a poor and dirty part of London.

“And how did you know me?” Hyde asked suddenly.

“We have friends in common. Dr Jekyll, for example.”

“He never told you about me!” Hyde cried angrily. “You're lying!” Then, with a wild laugh, he unlocked the door and disappeared inside.

Utterson stood in the street, shaking. “He hardly seems human,” he whispered. “Oh, my poor Harry Jekyll! If I ever saw the devil's name written on a face, it was on that one.”

Around the corner, in a quiet square of fine old houses, stood Dr Jekyll's home. Utterson knocked. Poole, the doctor's old butler, told him that his master was out.

“I've just seen Mr Hyde go in by that old door round the corner,” said Utterson. “Is that all right when your master is away?”

“The laboratory door? Quite all right, sir,” said Poole. “Mr Hyde has a key, and the master has told us all to obey him. But we hardly ever see him in the house.”

So the ugly door with no bell was the back door of Jekyll's laboratory — the old building behind his house where he did his scientific work.

Two weeks later Jekyll gave a dinner party. Utterson stayed behind after the other guests had gone.

“Jekyll, I don't like your will,” said Utterson. “I've been hearing things about young Hyde.”

Jekyll's face went pale, and something dark came into his eyes. “I don't want to talk about it. My position is very strange — very strange indeed. But believe me, the moment I choose, I can get rid of Mr Hyde. I give you my word. Only promise me this, Utterson: if anything happens to me, you will help him and see that he gets his rights.”

“I'll never like him,” said Utterson.

“I don't ask that. I only ask you to be fair to him when I'm no longer here.”

Utterson sighed. “Very well,” he said. “I promise.”

Nearly a year later, the whole of London was shocked by a terrible crime.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Murder in the Moonlight
chapters.text:
One night in October, a young maid was sitting alone at her bedroom window in a house near the river. The moon was full, and the street below was as bright as day.

She saw an old gentleman with beautiful white hair walking along the street. A very small man was coming towards him. The old gentleman stopped and spoke to him politely — perhaps he was asking the way. And the maid recognised the small man. It was a Mr Hyde, who had once visited her master.

Hyde was playing impatiently with a heavy walking stick. He did not answer. Then suddenly, like a wild animal, he exploded with anger. He knocked the old man to the ground with his stick. Then he jumped on him and hit him again and again, so hard that the maid heard the bones break. At this, she fainted.

When she woke up and called the police, the murderer was long gone. Next to the body lay half of a broken stick. In the dead man's pocket the police found a gold watch, some money — and a letter addressed to Mr Utterson.

Next morning Inspector Newcomen of Scotland Yard brought Utterson to see the body. The lawyer looked down and went pale. “Yes, I know him,” he said quietly. “This is Sir Danvers Carew.”

Sir Danvers was a member of Parliament and a much-loved man. But Utterson had a second shock when he saw the broken stick. Many years ago he had given that stick to Henry Jekyll as a present.

“The maid says the killer was a Mr Hyde,” said the inspector.

“Is he a small man?” asked Utterson. The inspector nodded. “Then come with me. I can show you where he lives.”

A thick brown fog lay over the city, and although it was morning, the streets of Soho were as dark as evening. An old woman with silver hair and an evil face opened the door of Hyde's house.

“Mr Hyde isn't at home,” she said. “He came in very late last night and went out again within the hour.”

Hyde's rooms were comfortable, but everything was in a mess. In the fireplace someone had burnt a pile of papers. Among the ashes the inspector found the remains of a cheque book. And behind the door stood the other half of the broken stick.

“I've got him!” he said happily. “He'll need money, and we'll be waiting for him at the bank.”

But Hyde had no friends, and there was no photograph of him. The few people who had seen him could not describe him. They remembered only the ugly, uneasy feeling that he left behind.

That afternoon Utterson went to Jekyll's house. Poole took him across the back yard, through the laboratory and up a staircase to the cabinet — Jekyll's private room. Jekyll was sitting close to the fire. He looked terribly ill, and he did not stand up.

“You've heard the news?” asked Utterson. Jekyll nodded weakly. “Then tell me one thing. You aren't mad enough to hide this man?”

“Utterson, I swear to God I will never see him again. He is safe, and he will never be heard of again. Look — he wrote to me. The letter came by hand this morning, not by post.”

He handed Utterson a letter in strange, sharp handwriting. Hyde wrote that Dr Jekyll did not need to worry about him. He had a sure way to escape. It was signed “Edward Hyde”.

On his way out, Utterson spoke to Poole. “By the way, Poole, a letter came by hand today. What did the messenger look like?”

Poole looked surprised. “Nobody came today, sir. Only the post.”

Back in his office, Utterson showed Hyde's letter to his head clerk, Mr Guest, an expert on handwriting. Just then a servant brought a short note from Dr Jekyll — an invitation to dinner.

Guest placed the two papers side by side and studied them for a long time. “Interesting,” he said. “The writing on the two papers is almost the same. Only the letters lean a different way.”

When Guest had gone, Utterson locked Hyde's letter in his safe. His blood ran cold.

“What!” he whispered. “Henry Jekyll writing false letters for a murderer?”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Face at the Window
chapters.text:
The police offered a large reward, but Mr Hyde had disappeared as if he had never existed.

And with Hyde gone, Dr Jekyll seemed to come back to life. He opened his doors to his friends again. He went to church, gave money to the poor and looked years younger. For two months he was at peace. On the eighth of January, Utterson and Dr Lanyon had dinner at his house, and the three old friends laughed together like schoolboys.

But on the twelfth of January, when Utterson called again, Poole met him at the door. “I'm sorry, sir. The doctor is not seeing anyone.” It was the same the next day, and the day after that.

Worried, Utterson went to see Dr Lanyon. Only a few days earlier Lanyon had been a cheerful, red-faced man. Now he was thin and grey, and his hands shook. He looked like a man who was going to die. But worse than that was the look in his eyes. It was the look of terror.

“I've had a shock,” said Lanyon, “and I shall never recover. It's a question of weeks.”

“Jekyll is ill too,” said Utterson. “Have you seen him?”

Lanyon's face changed. “I wish to see or hear no more of Dr Jekyll,” he said in a loud, trembling voice. “I've finished with him. Please, never speak to me again of a man I regard as dead.” He turned away. “Some day, Utterson, after I'm dead, perhaps you will learn the whole story. But I cannot tell you.”

Utterson went home and wrote to Jekyll at once. The answer was long and strange.

“Don't blame our old friend,” Jekyll wrote. “I agree that we must never meet. From now on I'm going to live alone. I have brought on myself a punishment and a danger that I cannot name. If I am the worst of sinners, I am also the worst of sufferers. You can do only one thing for me, Utterson: respect my silence.”

Less than three weeks later Lanyon was dead. After the funeral, Utterson locked himself in his office and took out an envelope that Lanyon had left for him. On it, in his dead friend's handwriting, were the words: “PRIVATE: for G. J. Utterson ALONE.”

Inside there was a second envelope. It said: “Not to be opened until the death or disappearance of Dr Henry Jekyll.”

Disappearance! The same word as in the mad will. Utterson wanted very much to open the envelope. But he was an honest lawyer, and he had to obey his friend's wishes. He put it unopened at the back of his safe.

One Sunday, during their usual walk, Utterson and Enfield found themselves in the small street with the ugly door.

“Well,” said Enfield, “that story is at an end. We'll never see Mr Hyde again.”

“I hope not,” said Utterson. “Did I tell you? I once saw him, and I felt exactly what you felt.”

“Everyone does. And by the way, I've found out that this door leads into Dr Jekyll's laboratory. Let's go into the yard and look at the windows.”

In the yard they looked up. One of the cabinet windows was half open, and Dr Jekyll was sitting close to it. He looked like a sad prisoner.

“Jekyll!” called Utterson. “I hope you're feeling better. Come out and take a walk with us.”

“I'd like to very much,” answered Jekyll. “But no, no, no, it's quite impossible. I don't dare.”

“Then let's talk from here.”

“That's just what I was going to suggest,” said Jekyll with a smile.

But the words had hardly left his mouth when the smile disappeared from his face. In its place came a look of such terror and such hopelessness that the two men below felt their blood freeze. The window was shut at once. They had seen that face for only a second, but it was enough.

They left the yard without a word. Only in the next street did Utterson look at Enfield. They were both as pale as death.

“God forgive us,” said Utterson. “God forgive us.”

Enfield only nodded, and they walked on in silence.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Last Night
chapters.text:
One evening in March, Poole arrived at Utterson's house. His face was white.

“Something is wrong with the doctor, sir,” he said. “I've been afraid for a week. Please come with me.”

It was a wild, cold night, and a pale moon lay on its back in the sky. In Jekyll's house the servants stood together in the hall like frightened sheep.

Poole led Utterson across the yard into the laboratory, climbed the stairs and knocked on the cabinet door. “Mr Utterson is here to see you, sir.”

A voice answered from inside. “Tell him I cannot see anyone.”

Then Poole led him back across the yard to the kitchen and turned to him. “Sir, was that my master's voice?”

“It seemed very much changed,” said Utterson.

“Changed? I've served him for twenty years. That was not his voice! Eight days ago I heard him cry out to God. I believe my master has been killed. And who is in there instead of him?”

All week the thing in the cabinet had been crying out for some medicine. Poole had taken its written orders to every chemist in London. But each time he brought the powder back, there was another note: it's not pure, take it back, find me some of the old kind.

Utterson looked at the last note. It was in Jekyll's handwriting, and at the end the pen had pressed so hard that it had torn the paper: “For God's sake, find me some of the old!”

“And I've seen him, sir!” said Poole. “Once, in the laboratory. When he saw me, he gave a cry like a rat and ran upstairs. He had a mask over his face. And sir — he was small. My master is a tall man. That thing was not my master. I believe it was Mr Hyde.”

Utterson was silent. Then he said, “I believe you, Poole. We must break down the door.”

Poole fetched an axe, and they waited in the dark laboratory. The wind moaned, and above them they could hear footsteps, going up and down, up and down.

“It walks like that all night,” whispered Poole. “And once I heard it crying, like a lost soul.”

At last Utterson went up the stairs. “Jekyll,” he called, “I demand to see you. If you won't open the door, we'll break it down.”

“Utterson,” said the voice, “for God's sake, have mercy!”

“That's not Jekyll's voice — it's Hyde's!” cried Utterson. “Down with the door, Poole!”

Poole swung the axe, and a scream of animal terror came from the cabinet. Four times the axe fell. At the fifth blow the door broke and fell inside.

The room was quiet and warm. A fire was burning, the kettle was singing, and tea things stood on the table. But in the middle of the floor lay the body of a man, and it was still moving a little.

They turned it over. It was Edward Hyde. He was wearing clothes that were far too big for him — Dr Jekyll's clothes. In his hand there was a broken bottle, and the air smelled of poison. He was dead.

“We've come too late,” said Utterson, “to save him or to punish him. Now we must find your master's body.”

They searched every room, and even the cellar. There was no Henry Jekyll, dead or alive.

On the desk lay a large envelope with Utterson's name on it. Inside was a new will — and the name in it was not Edward Hyde, but Gabriel John Utterson — his own name! There was also a short note in Jekyll's hand, written that same day.

“My dear Utterson,” it said, “when this falls into your hands, I shall have disappeared. Go and read the letter that Lanyon left you. Then, if you want to know more, read my confession. Your unhappy friend, Henry Jekyll.”

Next to it lay a thick packet — the confession. Utterson put it in his pocket.

“Say nothing to anyone, Poole,” he said. “I'll be back before midnight, and then we'll call the police.”

At home, he took Lanyon's envelope out of his safe with shaking hands. At last he was going to learn the truth.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Dr Lanyon's Story
chapters.text:
Utterson opened Lanyon's envelope and began to read.

On the ninth of January I received a letter from Henry Jekyll. This surprised me, because I had dined at his house only the night before. We were very old friends, although for years I had called his science dangerous nonsense.

The letter was wild and strange. Jekyll begged me to go to his house at once. Poole would be waiting there with a locksmith. I was to break open the door of the cabinet, take out the fourth drawer from the top and carry it home. At midnight I had to be alone in my study. A man would come to me in Jekyll's name, and I had to give him the drawer. “If you fail me,” Jekyll wrote, “you may be responsible for my death or the loss of my mind.”

I thought my poor friend was mad. But I did as he asked.

At home I looked into the drawer. There was a packet of white powder, like salt, and a small bottle of blood-red liquid with a sharp smell. There was also a notebook with dates and short notes. Next to one date Jekyll had written “double”. Next to another: “total failure!!!” Then I took out my old revolver and loaded it.

The clocks had hardly struck twelve when I heard a soft knock. I opened the door myself. A small man was standing in the shadows by the wall. When he saw a policeman coming along the street, he jumped and hurried inside.

In my study I saw him clearly. The moment I looked at him, my skin went cold. His clothes were good, but they were much too big for him. His trousers were rolled up at the bottom, and his coat hung loose around his neck. On another man it would have looked funny. On him it was horrible.

“Have you got it?” he cried, and he put his hand on my arm.

I pushed him back. “You forget, sir, that I have not yet had the pleasure of knowing you. Please sit down.”

“I beg your pardon, Dr Lanyon,” he said. His voice was shaking. “I'm in a great hurry. Dr Jekyll sent me for a certain drawer …”

I pointed to it. He rushed to it like a hungry animal and gave a sob of such relief that I sat frozen in my chair.

He asked for a glass, poured in some of the red liquid and added the powder. The mixture began to bubble and smoke. Then it turned dark purple, and then, slowly, a pale, watery green.

My visitor held up the glass. “And now,” he said, “will you be wise? Will you let me take this glass and go? Or are you too curious? Think before you answer. If you choose, a new world of knowledge and power will open before your eyes.”

“I have gone too far to stop now,” I said. “I want to see the end.”

“Very well,” he said. “Lanyon, you laughed at my science. You called it nonsense. Now — look!”

He put the glass to his lips and drank it in one swallow.

A terrible cry followed. He held on to the table and stared at me with wild, red eyes. And as I watched, he began to change. His body seemed to grow. His face went black, and then it seemed to melt and take a new shape.

The next moment I was on my feet, with my back to the wall and my arm in front of my face. “Oh God!” I screamed, again and again. “Oh God!”

Because there before my eyes — pale and shaking, feeling his way with his hands like a man who has come back from the dead — there stood Henry Jekyll!

What he told me in the next hour, I cannot write. I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul is sick. I shall die soon. One thing more, Utterson. The creature who came into my house that night was, as Jekyll himself told me, known by the name of Hyde — the man hunted all over England for the murder of Carew.

Hastie Lanyon

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Henry Jekyll's Confession
chapters.text:
Then Utterson opened Jekyll's packet and read his friend's last words.

I was born rich and clever, and I wanted the respect of good men. But another side of me loved wild pleasures, and I hid it in shame. So I lived a double life.

Slowly I understood a great truth: man is not one, but two. In each of us, good and evil live side by side. What if I could separate them? Then the good side could live without shame, and the evil side could go its own way.

After many experiments, I found the right mixture. One part of it was a special salt, and I bought a large amount. Late one night I mixed the drink and swallowed it.

The pain was terrible, as if my bones were breaking. Then it passed, and I felt young, light, happy and wicked. It was like strong wine. I looked down. My body had grown smaller.

I crept to my bedroom and looked in the mirror. For the first time I saw Edward Hyde. And I was not afraid. This, too, was myself. He was smaller and younger than Jekyll, because for most of my life my evil side had been hidden away, with little chance to grow. His face was pure evil, and that is why everyone hated him at first sight.

I drank the mixture again and became Jekyll once more.

By day I was the respected Dr Jekyll. At night I could become Hyde, free to do anything. I took the house in Soho, told my servants to obey Mr Hyde and wrote that will. At first Hyde's pleasures were only foolish. Soon they became cruel. You know the story of the little girl. I paid for it with my own cheque.

Then one morning I woke up in my bed and saw my hand on the sheet. It was not the large white hand of Henry Jekyll. It was thin, dark and hairy — the hand of Edward Hyde! I had gone to sleep as Jekyll and woken up as Hyde, without the drink.

Hyde was growing stronger. More and more often I needed a double amount of the drink to become Jekyll again. I had to choose, and I chose Jekyll. For two months I never touched the drink.

But the devil inside me had been locked up too long. One night I drank again, and Hyde came out roaring. That was the night I met Sir Danvers Carew. I hit him again and again, and I enjoyed every blow. Then fear came. I ran to Soho, burned my papers and escaped. Back in my cabinet I drank the mixture and, Jekyll once more, fell on my knees and cried to God.

Now Hyde was a murderer, hunted by every policeman in London. He had to disappear forever. For a while I lived a good, quiet life.

Then, one fine January day, I was sitting on a bench in Regent's Park. Suddenly I felt sick. I looked down at my hand. It was Hyde's! I could not go home — my own servants would call the police. So I took a room in a small hotel, and there, with Hyde's hand, I wrote to Lanyon in Jekyll's handwriting. You know the rest. The shock killed him.

Now Hyde comes whenever he wants. If I fall asleep for a moment, I wake up as him. Only a double amount brings me back, and only for a short time. And now my salt has run out. I sent Poole to every chemist in London, but the new salt doesn't work. My first salt, I now understand, was not pure, and that impurity was the secret. And there is no more of it.

The last of the old powder has made me Jekyll for one more hour, and I am using it to write this. Soon I shall be Edward Hyde again, and this time forever. Will Hyde be hanged for murder? Or will he find the courage to kill himself? God knows, and I do not care. This is my true hour of death. What happens next will happen to another man.

And so, as I put down my pen, I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.
